Administer 500 mg of levofloxacin orally or intravenously once daily for 7 to 14 days, or 750 mg orally or intravenously once daily for 5 days, depending on the clinical indication and severity of the infection. 2. For acute sinusitis, use fluoroquinolones only when no other treatment options are available. 3. For acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, administer 500 mg orally or intravenously once daily for at least 7 days. Reserve fluoroquinolones for patients without alternative treatment options. 4. For post-exposure therapy, administer 500 mg orally once daily for 60 days, starting as soon as possible after exposure. 5. For uncomplicated infections, administer 500 mg orally or intravenously once daily for 7 to 10 days. For complicated infections, administer 750 mg orally or intravenously once daily for 7 to 14 days. 6. For chronic infections, administer 500 mg orally or intravenously once daily for 28 days. 7. For uncomplicated urinary tract infections, administer 250 mg orally or intravenously once daily for 10 days or 750 mg orally or intravenously once daily for 5 days. Reserve fluoroquinolones for patients without alternative treatment options. 8. For treatment and prophylaxis of plague (including pneumonic and septicemic plague) caused by Yersinia pestis, administer 500 mg orally or intravenously once daily for 10 to 14 days in adults and pediatric patients aged 6 months or older. 9. For pediatric patients weighing less than 30 kg, tablets are not recommended due to limitations in available strengths. Consider alternative formulations of levofloxacin. 10. For post-exposure therapy in pediatric patients aged 6 months and weighing less than 50 kg, administer 8 mg/kg orally every 12 hours for 60 days, not exceeding 250 mg per dose. For those weighing more than 50 kg, administer 500 mg orally once daily for 60 days. 11. Safety of levofloxacin in children for treatment durations exceeding 14 days has not been established. 12. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with drugs that prolong the QTc interval, such as amiodarone, amisulpride, arsenic trioxide, and others, due to the increased risk of torsades de pointes and other serious arrhythmias. If co-administration is unavoidable, monitor ECGs and electrolytes closely. 13. Aluminum hydroxide decreases levofloxacin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Avoid or separate administration by at least 2 hours. 14. Aminolevulinic acid (oral or topical) increases the phototoxicity of levofloxacin. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 15. Live bacterial vaccines, such as BCG or typhoid vaccine, are contraindicated during levofloxacin therapy due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Wait until antibiotic therapy is complete before administering live vaccines. 16. Drugs like ferrous sulfate, ferrous fumarate, and ferric maltol reduce levofloxacin absorption when co-administered orally. Avoid or separate administration by at least 2 hours. 17. Ondansetron and levofloxacin both prolong the QTc interval. Avoid co-administration in patients with congenital long QT syndrome or other risk factors. Monitor ECGs if used together. 18. Drugs such as panobinostat, vandetanib, and vemurafenib significantly prolong the QTc interval. Avoid co-administration with levofloxacin or monitor ECGs closely if unavoidable. 19. Levofloxacin may increase the risk of dysglycemia (hyperor hypoglycemia) when co-administered with antidiabetic agents like acarbose. Monitor blood glucose levels closely. 20. Co-administration of levofloxacin with adrenergic agonists like albuterol may potentiate cardiovascular effects. Use caution and monitor. 21. Levofloxacin increases the phototoxicity of retinoids like tretinoin (oral or topical). Avoid co-administration or use alternative therapies. 22. Drugs like sodium bicarbonate and sodium citrate reduce levofloxacin absorption when co-administered orally. Avoid or separate administration by at least 2 hours. 23. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with QTc-prolonging agents such as sotalol, quinidine, or procainamide. Monitor ECGs if co-administration is unavoidable. 24. Levofloxacin may increase the toxicity of umeclidinium/vilanterol inhaled by prolonging the QTc interval. Use extreme caution and monitor cardiovascular effects. 25. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with drugs like selinexor, which may cause neurological toxicities. Monitor for dizziness or confusion if used together. 26. Levofloxacin decreases the efficacy of microbiota oral therapy due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Complete antibiotic therapy 2 to 4 days before initiating microbiota oral therapy. 27. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with drugs like trilaciclib, which may increase the risk of serious toxicities due to renal or systemic accumulation. 28. Exercise caution when using levofloxacin with adrenergic agonists or other QTc-prolonging agents, and monitor for cardiovascular effects. 29. Avoid concurrent use of levofloxacin with drugs like torsemide or tetrabenazine, which may increase the risk of QTc prolongation. Monitor ECGs if co-administration is unavoidable. 30. Levofloxacin increases the phototoxicity of methyl aminolevulinate. Avoid co-administration or use alternative therapies. 31. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with live vaccines like cholera vaccine, as systemic antibiotics may reduce vaccine efficacy. Wait at least 14 days after completing antibiotics before administering the vaccine. 32. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with QTc-prolonging agents like ribociclib, as this may increase the risk of torsades de pointes. Monitor ECGs if co-administration is unavoidable. 33. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with drugs like sevoflurane or siponimod, which may prolong the QTc interval. Use alternative therapies or monitor ECGs closely. 34. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with drugs like oxaliplatin or pentamidine, which may increase the risk of QTc prolongation. Monitor ECGs if co-administration is unavoidable. 35. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with drugs like pimozide or pitolisant, which may increase the risk of QTc prolongation. Monitor ECGs if co-administration is unavoidable. 36. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with drugs like typhoid vaccine live, as systemic antibiotics may reduce vaccine efficacy. Wait until antibiotic therapy is complete before administering the vaccine. 37. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with drugs like vandetanib or vemurafenib, which may increase the risk of QTc prolongation. Monitor ECGs if co-administration is unavoidable. 38. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with drugs like vilanterol/fluticasone furoate inhaled, as this may increase cardiovascular toxicity. Monitor for QTc prolongation and cardiovascular effects. 39. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with drugs like albuterol or alfuzosin, which may increase the risk of QTc prolongation. Monitor ECGs if co-administration is unavoidable. 40. Avoid co-administration of levofloxacin with drugs like amifampridine, which may increase toxicity. Modify therapy or monitor closely.
